job.style: a diary entry or letter by a student

passage: Dear Diary, today in biology class, we learned that respiration is a cellular process, not just the physical act of breathing. My teacher explained that while we breathe to take in air, our cells use oxygen to break down glucose for energy. It is fascinating that even yeast, which we use to make bread rise, performs this process constantly to survive, not just when baking. We also discussed how fish survive underwater; they do not break down water molecules, but instead extract dissolved oxygen from the water using their gills. I was surprised to learn that plants also respire through tiny pores called stomata, which handle gas exchange for both respiration and transpiration. Finally, we looked at human muscles during exercise. When we run hard, our muscles do not stop respiring; instead, they switch to anaerobic respiration, which produces lactic acid because oxygen supply cannot keep up with the high energy demand. It is clear now that respiration is a fundamental energy-releasing process occurring in all living cells, whether in a tiny yeast cell, a plant leaf, or our own hardworking muscles.

items.evidence: We also discussed how fish survive underwater; they do not break down water molecules, but instead extract dissolved oxygen from the water using their gills.
items.q: How does a fish get the oxygen it needs underwater?
options: Its gills take in oxygen dissolved in water
Its cells split water into hydrogen and oxygen
Its mouth swallows air from the surface
Its gills turn carbon dioxide into oxygen
items.explain: Fish do not split water; their gills extract the oxygen already dissolved in it.

wrong.why: thinks fish break down H2O to get oxygen
thinks animals always breathe through the mouth like humans
thinks respiration makes oxygen for the body

items.evidence: It is fascinating that even yeast, which we use to make bread rise, performs this process constantly to survive, not just when baking.
items.q: A packet of yeast sits unused in a kitchen cupboard, alive. What is its respiration doing?
options: It continues all the time to keep it alive
It starts only once dough is added
It stops until the yeast is heated
It happens only in the yeast's lungs
items.explain: Yeast respires constantly to survive, not only when it is used for baking.

wrong.why: thinks yeast respires only when making bread rise
thinks respiration needs a breathing action first
thinks respiration happens only in lungs

items.evidence: I was surprised to learn that plants also respire through tiny pores called stomata, which handle gas exchange for both respiration and transpiration.
items.q: A student says stomata only let water out of a leaf. What is wrong with this?
options: They also exchange gases used in respiration
They let water out only at night
They let in water for the roots
They only open when a plant respires
items.explain: Stomata handle gas exchange for respiration as well as transpiration, so water loss is not their only job.

wrong.why: repeats the idea that stomata only release water
adds a time rule not given in the passage
confuses stomata with root water uptake

items.evidence: When we run hard, our muscles do not stop respiring; instead, they switch to anaerobic respiration, which produces lactic acid because oxygen supply cannot keep up with the high energy demand.
items.q: Why do muscles make lactic acid during a hard run?
options: Oxygen supply is too low for the demand
Their cells stop respiring to rest
Their cells make extra oxygen for energy
Anaerobic respiration is as efficient as aerobic
items.explain: Oxygen cannot keep up with the energy demand, so muscles switch to anaerobic respiration, which makes lactic acid.

wrong.why: thinks the body stops respiring during exercise
thinks respiration makes oxygen for the body
thinks anaerobic respiration is as efficient as aerobic
